subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage: On Monday morning in the corridor of her Bengaluru school, Vidya caught Irawati glancing at her sideways and then quickly looking at the floor. Irawati leaned towards Shreya and whispered. Vidya's face went hot. It had to be the fringe; she had cut it herself on Sunday. All through maths she drafted a sharp message in her head. At lunch she nearly walked past their table without a word. Instead she stopped. "Irawati, were you two talking about me this morning?" Irawati turned red. "Sort of. We wanted to ask if you'd sing in our band for the fest. I didn't know how to ask, so I kept looking and then lost my nerve." Shreya laughed. "She practised the question three times." Vidya sat down slowly, the sharp message gone.

qa.q: When had Vidya cut her fringe?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when her face went hot?
qa.a: Vidya felt embarrassed and angry, sure that Irawati was whispering about the home-cut fringe.

qa.q: What stopped this from turning into a needless fight?
qa.a: Vidya asked Irawati directly instead of sending the sharp message or walking past, and the real reason came out 🙂

qa.q: How did Irawati experience that morning?
qa.a: Irawati was shy and nervous about asking Vidya to sing, so she kept glancing over and then lost her nerve.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reading sideways glances as gossip when they came from shyness, and checking the facts instead of assuming the worst.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Tuesday
When I read out the debate results, Anirban's cheeks rose into a wide grin as his team's name came first. A second later, when I added that his closing speech was the best of the day, his whole face went red up to the ears, and he looked down at his desk. Ritu called out, "Tomato alert!" and a few students laughed. Anirban's shoulders came up and the grin vanished. I said, "Going red just means something matters to you. Ritu, you went pink too when your team was called." That got a laugh that included both of them. Later Anirban told me he hates how easily he blushes. Next step: I will praise him privately more often, and I have asked Ritu to help lead Friday's warm-up, where her quick wit can be put to kind use.

qa.q: Which part of Anirban's work did the teacher call the best of the day?
qa.a: His closing speech.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when his face went red and he looked down?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed even while proud, because the praise came in front of the whole class.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to spare Anirban?
qa.a: The teacher turned the joke into something shared, explained blushing kindly, and planned to praise Anirban privately in future.

qa.q: How might Ritu have meant "Tomato alert!"?
qa.a: Ritu probably meant it as a joke, but for Anirban, already self-conscious, it stung and wiped away his grin.

grounding: It shows a teenager's raised cheeks of real pleasure turning into a blush of embarrassment, and an adult reading the context and sparing him kindly.

passage: I'm Kabir, Mahima's brother, and I was in the kitchen when Ayesha brought over the karela chutney she'd made for her cooking project. She was so proud she carried the jar with both hands. Mahima took a spoonful. I saw her nose start to wrinkle, the way it does when she smells my football socks. Then she stopped it. She pressed her lips together, swallowed, and her face went smooth. "Okay, honest opinion?" she said. "It's really bitter for me. But the garlic is amazing, and I'd eat it with curd rice." Ayesha laughed. "Everyone says it's bitter! Karela is bitter!" I can't know what Mahima really felt, but her face never sneered, and Ayesha left smiling with the half-empty jar.

qa.q: What had Ayesha made for her cooking project?
qa.a: Karela chutney.

qa.q: What might Mahima's pressed lips and smoothed face suggest?
qa.a: Mahima probably felt a flash of disgust at the bitterness, but also cared about not hurting Ayesha, who was so proud of it.

qa.q: What made Mahima's response both kind and honest?
qa.a: She softened the face, then used words: named the bitterness honestly, praised the garlic and said how she'd enjoy it.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt if Mahima had just sneered?
qa.a: Ayesha would likely have felt hurt and embarrassed about the project she carried so proudly, without knowing what exactly was wrong.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager softening a disgust nose wrinkle at a friend's cooking and giving an honest opinion kindly in words, seen by a sibling.

subtype: Lip biting when unsure or anxious [Regulating]
passage:
Tuesday: In the project meeting, Aarav told Ms Pinto that the model's wiring was his idea. Devika bit her lower lip so hard it went white, and said nothing.
Thursday: When Ms Pinto praised "Aarav's circuit" in class, Devika's teeth caught her lip again. Gurleen noticed. At the bus stop she asked softly, "You keep biting your lip when the project comes up. Want to talk, or leave it?" Devika let go of her lip. "The wiring was mine. If I say so, I'll sound jealous." Gurleen shook her head. "Or you'll sound like the person who did the wiring."
Monday: Devika took her dated sketches of the wiring diagram to Ms Pinto. Her voice shook a little, but her lip stayed free. Ms Pinto listened and changed the credits to show both names.

qa.q: What did Devika take to Ms Pinto on Monday?
qa.a: Her dated sketches of the wiring diagram.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when she bit her lip on Tuesday?
qa.a: She felt angry and hurt that Aarav took the credit, but held back her words, worried about sounding jealous.

qa.q: What helped Devika speak up instead of biting back the words?
qa.a: Gurleen's gentle, no-pressure question, a new way to see it, and bringing dated sketches as evidence to Ms Pinto.

qa.q: How did Gurleen read Devika's lip biting?
qa.a: Gurleen saw it as a sign that Devika was holding something back, and offered a gentle question with the choice to leave it.

grounding: It shows a teenager biting the lip to hold back words and calm nerves, and a friend noticing it and opening a gentle question.

subtype: Pouting and pursing for cameras and moods [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Urmila, and I've shared a desk with Vandana since Class 7, so I've seen a lot of her pouts. At the school fete she did her selfie pout, lips pushed out, cheeks sucked in, and then laughed at the picture. That's a style, not a mood. But on Saturday, when the group photo from Shreya's birthday went up and Vandana wasn't in it because she hadn't been invited, her lips pushed out the same way. Only this time there was no phone. Her eyes were fixed on the floor, and she didn't laugh. Kunal said, "Ooh, duck face again," and she walked off. I couldn't be sure what she felt, but I went after her. I didn't mention the photo. I just sat with her on the stairs until lunch ended.

qa.q: Since which class have Urmila and Vandana shared a desk?
qa.a: Since Class 7.

qa.q: What might Vandana's pout on Saturday suggest?
qa.a: It probably showed real hurt and sadness at being left out of Shreya's birthday, since her eyes were down and she didn't laugh.

qa.q: How did Urmila help?
qa.a: Urmila followed Vandana and sat quietly without raising the photo, offering company instead of questions.

qa.q: What would change if Kunal had noticed the context before joking?
qa.a: He might have seen Vandana was hurt, not posing, and held back the 'duck face' joke that deepened the hurt.

grounding: It illustrates the same pout as a selfie style and as a real sulk, with context telling them apart and mockery deepening the hurt, seen by a deskmate.

passage:
Sunday night
My jaw aches. I noticed it in the chemistry mock this afternoon when question 4 made no sense: my teeth were locked so hard my ears buzzed. Then at dinner Uma didi said, in front of everyone, that I spend more time on my phone than on revision, and my jaw locked again. I didn't say what I wanted to say. I just chewed my roti like it had done something wrong.
After dinner Papa found me on the terrace. He didn't ask what happened. He said, "You look like you're holding a lot in your face. I'm here if you want to talk, or not." Then he showed me a silly trick: open your mouth wide like a lion, slide your jaw side to side, breathe out slowly. I did it three times and felt my shoulders drop. I told him a bit about the mock. Not about didi, yet.
Rashmi

qa.q: Which question in the mock made no sense?
qa.a: Question 4.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when the jaw locked again at dinner?
qa.a: Rashmi felt angry and embarrassed at being criticised by Uma didi in front of everyone, but held the words back.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi's tension ease?
qa.a: Papa's no-pressure offer to talk, plus the lion stretch and slow breathing, which let the shoulders drop and some of the day come out.

qa.q: How might Papa have read Rashmi's face on the terrace?
qa.a: Papa saw tension held in the face and chose to offer company and a trick instead of questions.

grounding: It shows a teenager clenching the jaw under exam and family pressure to hold back words, eased by a jaw stretch, slow breathing and a parent's no-pressure offer to talk.

subtype: Moving the jaw sideways and tongue clicks [Mismatch]
passage: In the tuition centre above a sweet shop in Indore, Kishore stared at the geometry problem, shifting his jaw from side to side. Ishita suggested, "What if we draw the diagonal?" Kishore clicked his tongue: tch. Ishita's eyes narrowed. "Wow. Okay. Forget it." Kishore looked up, puzzled. "What?" "You just went tch at my idea." "No! I was clicking at myself. I hadn't seen the diagonal. That was a why-didn't-I-think-of-that tch." Ishita folded her arms. "It sounded exactly like the tch my brother does when he thinks I'm being stupid." Kishore considered that. "Fair. My mum says the same about my tch. Next time I'll just say 'good idea' out loud." He drew the diagonal. It worked.

qa.q: Where was the tuition centre?
qa.a: Above a sweet shop in Indore.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when her eyes narrowed?
qa.a: She felt dismissed and annoyed, taking Kishore's tongue click as scorn for her idea.

qa.q: What fix did Kishore choose, and why might it help?
qa.a: Saying 'good idea' out loud, because words are clearer than a click that can sound dismissive.

qa.q: How did Kishore see his own tongue click?
qa.a: To Kishore it was a click at himself, a 'why didn't I think of that', not a judgement on Ishita.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager's sideways jaw and tongue click meaning thought to him but attitude to a peer, with tone and relationship deciding the meaning.

passage: At the kabaddi tournament in Sonpur, Uday stood at the line with his face perfectly still. Inside, his heart was hammering; he had practised that blank look in the pond's reflection so the other team wouldn't see his nerves. On the bench, Minakshi, who had moved from the city in June, watched with her usual expression: mouth flat, brows slightly low. The girls near her whispered that she thought she was too good for the village. At half-time Uday flopped down beside her. "You look like you hate kabaddi." Minakshi blinked. "I'm loving it. This is just my face. My mother says I look cross even when I'm reading." Uday laughed. "And I look calm when I'm scared stiff." Minakshi grinned properly for the first time and moved over to share the shade.

qa.q: Where had Uday practised his blank look?
qa.a: In the pond's reflection.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling behind his still face?
qa.a: He was nervous, with his heart hammering, but hid it so the other team would think he was cool.

qa.q: What cleared up the misreading of Minakshi?
qa.a: Uday asked her directly, and she explained it was just her resting face; asking beat guessing.

qa.q: How did the girls on the bench read Minakshi's face?
qa.a: They took her flat mouth and low brows as pride, thinking she felt too good for the village, when she was actually enjoying the match.

grounding: It shows one teenager's deliberate poker face hiding nerves and another's resting face looking unfriendly, with neither proving coldness and asking clearing it up.

subtype: Tense or rigid face under threat [Interpreting]
passage:
Swati: I saw your face when you read that message in the library. You went totally still.
Hrithik: sorry I just walked off
Swati: don't be sorry. you don't have to explain anything
Hrithik: Dadu had a fall. he's in hospital. Mum's there now
Hrithik: I didn't cry or anything. Pranav said I looked like I didn't care
Swati: you looked frozen, not like you didn't care. shock can look like that
Hrithik: I still feel frozen
Swati: that's okay. want me to call, or just stay here on chat?
Hrithik: just stay
Swati: I'm here. is anyone home with you?
Hrithik: Papa's coming back from the hospital at 8. we'll eat together
Swati: ok. I'm online till you sleep. no need to reply

qa.q: Who had a fall?
qa.a: Hrithik's Dadu.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he said he still felt frozen?
qa.a: He was in shock and frightened about Dadu, numb rather than uncaring.

qa.q: What made Swati's support helpful?
qa.a: She named what she saw without judging, didn't demand an explanation, offered choices, checked someone would be home, and simply stayed.

qa.q: How did Pranav read Hrithik's still face?
qa.a: Pranav took it as not caring, missing that shock can freeze a face.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reading a friend's frozen face after upsetting news as shock or fear rather than indifference, and offering quiet support.

passage:
Exchange coordinator's note, day 3
Afreen arrived from Leicester on Monday to stay with Jyoti's family for the school exchange. Today at the canteen, Afreen asked the counter aunty whether the samosas had peas. The aunty tilted her head side to side, and Afreen put the samosa back, looking confused. Jyoti burst out laughing, then stopped when Afreen's face fell. "That wobble was a yes," Jyoti explained. "Or an okay. Sometimes it means I'm listening." Afreen asked, "So how do I know which?" Jyoti admitted, "Honestly, from the face and the situation. If you're not sure, just ask again." Afreen did, and the aunty said, "Haan, peas, peas," laughing. Next step: I am adding a short session on everyday gestures for the next group of visitors.

qa.q: Where had Afreen come from?
qa.a: Leicester.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she put the samosa back?
qa.a: Afreen felt confused, reading the side-to-side tilt as a possible no, and then a little embarrassed when Jyoti laughed.

qa.q: What advice did Jyoti give, and why does it work?
qa.a: Read the wobble from the face and the situation, and if unsure just ask again; asking removes the guesswork 👍

qa.q: How might Jyoti have seen the moment?
qa.a: To Jyoti the wobble was an obvious yes, so the mix-up seemed funny until she saw Afreen's face fall.

grounding: It shows a visiting teenager misreading the Indian head wobble as a no, and learning that it can mean yes, okay or listening and that asking again helps.
